paras: The whipping of Henry Meredith took place on the night of Saturday, June 13, 1903, at Armstrong, Missouri, when a group of citizens broke open the city jail, took out Meredith, a Black youth held on a charge of cutting another Black boy, and gave him 150 lashes with a harness tug. Meredith was not killed, and no arrests of the men who whipped him were reported. Missouri and Kansas papers carried the story as a short item, and the fuller accounts presented the whipping as a community's answer to lawlessness.

Constable Morehead arrested Meredith, described as "a negro boy," on Saturday on a charge of cutting Will Boggs, also Black. According to the Mexico Message, Meredith had cut Boggs badly with a knife and had attacked him "without any cause." Both the St. Louis Republic and the Message added that he had just served a term in the State Reform School at Boonville for attempting to wreck an Alton passenger train by piling railroad ties on the track.

That night a party the papers called "a posse of citizens" broke open the jail door and took Meredith about half a mile from town. There they stripped off his outer clothing, tied him to a telegraph pole and gave him 150 lashes with a harness tug. None of the reports names the men, gives their number or states their race.
No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry or any official response to the jail-breaking appears in the coverage, nor any report of Meredith's own trial.

The St. Louis Republic printed a special dispatch from Armstrong on June 15 under the headline "Mob Whips a Negro Boy. Armstrong Citizens Tire of Disregard for the Law." The same issue's front-page digest reduced the story to one sentence about a mob whipping a young Black man who "recently had committed numerous depredations," wording repeated by the Chariton Courier at Keytesville on June 19. A wire paragraph headed "A Negro Whipped with Harness Tugs" ran in the Kinsley Graphic and the Barton County Democrat in Kansas on June 19, and the Butler Weekly Times printed a similar short item on June 18.

The Mexico Message, which ran the item on June 25 as "Negro Criminal Whipped by a Posse," called Meredith "a notorious negro boy" and stressed that his attack on Boggs had no cause. None of the white papers condemned the breaking of the jail, and the fuller accounts placed his reform-school record beside the whipping. No Black-press coverage of the episode was found.

reader.title: Whipping of Henry Meredith
bases: A group of citizens broke into the town jail, took a Black prisoner out and whipped him severely; no killing, threat to kill or organized band is reported (A1, A3, A7).

The Republic special (A1) and the Mexico Message item (A7), which carries details and wording not in A1, agree on the victim, the jail-taking and the 150 lashes, and digests and wire items in other papers report the same core event (A2, A3, A6).

accounts.label: Republic special correspondent
accounts.gist: A posse of citizens broke open the city jail, took Meredith half a mile from town, stripped his outer garments, tied him to a telegraph pole and gave him 150 lashes; the headline presented it as citizens tiring of 'disregard for the law'.

accounts.label: Mexico Message state item
accounts.gist: Meredith, 'a notorious negro boy', was awaiting trial for cutting William Boggs, whom he had attacked 'without any cause', when a posse took him from jail and whipped him.

accounts.label: News digests
accounts.gist: A mob broke down the jail door and whipped an unnamed young Black prisoner said to have committed 'numerous depredations'.

framing.detail: The Republic headed its special 'Mob Whips a Negro Boy. Armstrong Citizens Tire of Disregard for the Law' and closed with Meredith's reform-school record.
The Mexico Message headed its item 'Negro Criminal Whipped by a Posse' and called Meredith 'notorious'.
Digest and wire items reported the jail-breaking and whipping in one or two sentences without comment.

versions.value: Charged with cutting Will Boggs, another Black boy

conflicts.note: The digests are one-sentence summaries without the victim's name; the named reports, including the Republic's own special from Armstrong, give the specific charge, which is the better evidence.
Different words for the same unnamed group; no paper reports that officers organized or led it.
